# Scenario — Meeting 3: Product Brainstorm

**Frozen design specification, written before the transcript and ground truth.**

## Meeting purpose

A loose, idea-heavy brainstorm about improving the weekly "digest" email feature. The whole point
of this meeting, by design, is that it generates a lot of talk and very little real commitment —
this is the suite's precision stress test: an extraction system that's trigger-happy about turning
discussion into tasks should fail badly here.

## Participants

- **Jordan** — product manager, loosely facilitates
- **Riley** — designer
- **Sana** — engineer
- **Felix** — engineer

## Intended active commitments (deliberately only 3)

1. **Sana will build a quick, rough prototype of a "trend graph" view** (showing activity trends
   over time) to see if it's even feasible, before anyone decides whether to build it properly.
2. **Riley will mock up two different layout options** for the digest email for the next design
   review.
3. **Felix will dogfood the digest feature with his own team** for a week as an informal
   experiment, to get a read on whether a Slack-delivery version is worth pursuing — a test/
   experiment action, not a build commitment.

## Intended negatives

1. **Suggestion nobody accepts:** someone proposes building an AI-generated activity-summary
   dashboard. It gets genuine back-and-forth discussion, but nobody ends up owning it or agreeing
   to do it — it is left exactly where every other unaccepted idea in this meeting is left.
2. **Hypothetical that sounds task-like but isn't real work:** someone walks through a detailed,
   vivid hypothetical ("imagine a user logs in Monday morning and sees everything sorted by
   project...") purely to illustrate a vision, not as something anyone is doing.
3. **Future feature explicitly deferred:** a Slack-integration delivery option for the digest is
   raised, discussed with real interest, and explicitly tabled for "next quarter at the earliest" —
   not started, not assigned, not scheduled.

## Tricky cases

- The meeting should contain many more speculative turns of phrasing ("we could," "what if,"
  "maybe," "I wonder if") than real commitments — roughly 8-10 distinct hypothetical/speculative
  ideas get aired for every 3 that land as commitments.
- Felix's "dogfood test" commitment (#3) must read as a genuine, scoped, agreed action ("yeah I'll
  just turn it on for my team and see") and not get confused with the surrounding pile of "what if
  someone tried..." speculation it's embedded in.
- The AI-dashboard idea (negative #1) gets unusually serious engagement (people genuinely debate
  it for several turns) before fizzling out with no owner — tests that depth of discussion alone
  doesn't imply commitment.
- The Slack-integration idea (negative #3) is popular enough that someone almost volunteers for it
  before Jordan explicitly tables it ("let's shelve that for now, next quarter at the earliest") —
  tests that an idea can be seriously considered and still correctly resolve to "not now."

## Ownership changes

None (this meeting has very little ownership of anything, by design).

## Dependency relationships

None.

## Transcript-noise plan

High density of hedging language and tangential product opinions ("I just don't think people read
digest emails anyway"). Light filler, a couple of people talking over each other when excited
about an idea. No ASR corruption in this meeting.

## Target size

Roughly 55–75 transcript segments; ~12–15 minutes of conversation.
